scenarios.title: Food delivery app breakdown into tasks
scenarios.prompt:
We're starting a food delivery app next sprint and I have 4 engineers. Can you break this down into implementation tasks? Here's the design summary and stories.

Design: React Native customer app, a Node/Postgres backend with REST API, a restaurant tablet web app, Stripe for payments, Twilio for SMS.

Stories:
S1 Customer browses restaurants by cuisine and location
S2 Customer views a menu and adds items to a cart
S3 Customer pays by card and gets a receipt
S4 Customer tracks order status live
S5 Restaurant staff accept or reject incoming orders
S6 Restaurant staff edit menu items and mark items sold out
S7 Customer receives SMS when the order status changes
S8 Customer rates an order after delivery

Thanks, need it by end of day.
rubric: Splits the work into end-to-end slices such as browsing/menu, checkout and payment, order tracking, and restaurant-side order handling, each carrying its own backend and UI parts, rather than listing database, backend, API and mobile app as separate work areas.
Every one of the eight stories (browse, cart, pay, track, accept/reject, menu editing, SMS, rating) is placed in at least one feature, including the easy-to-forget rating and SMS stories.
Notes that the order entity and its status are touched by checkout, tracking, restaurant handling and SMS, and either merges those or names a common order contract to settle first.
Gives a suggested sequence or effort view for the four engineers, saying which shared contract (such as order status or menu data) is agreed before the rest begin.
Each proposed slice can be checked on its own, for example by stubbing Stripe or Twilio or using a mock order, without waiting for other slices.
Presents the split as a proposal and asks the user to confirm or adjust before it is treated as final.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: A plain "break this down into implementation tasks" request for a multi-component app invites a layer-by-layer breakdown. The order entity is shared by several stories, and the story set includes minor ones that are easy to drop.

scenarios.title: Mutual calls between billing and entitlements
scenarios.prompt:
Need to split our SaaS subscription revamp across the team. Here's the HLD excerpt, please decompose into features for individual engineers.

Components:
- Billing service: creates subscriptions, handles upgrades/downgrades, issues invoices. On upgrade it calls Entitlements to grant the new plan's limits immediately. On failed payment it calls Entitlements to suspend features.
- Entitlements service: stores what each account may use (seats, API quota, modules). When a user hits a limit it calls Billing's "quote upgrade" endpoint to show the price in the in-app upsell dialog. On trial expiry it calls Billing to create the first invoice.
- Admin console: support staff can view and override subscriptions and entitlements.
- Usage metering: counts API calls per account, feeds Entitlements.

Stories:
A1 Customer upgrades or downgrades plan
A2 Customer is suspended after failed payment and restored after paying
A3 Customer sees an upsell quote when hitting a quota
A4 Trial converts to paid automatically at expiry
A5 Support staff overrides a customer's limits
A6 API usage is counted and shown to customer
A7 Customer downloads past invoices
rubric: Spots that billing and entitlements call each other (upgrade and suspension from billing, quote and trial invoice from entitlements) and does not hand them out as two features that wait on each other; resolves it by merging them or extracting a plan/limits contract that both sides use.
Identifies the plan/limit data or quote and grant endpoints as the thing several features rely on and says which features use it and that it is settled before work starts.
All seven stories A1 to A7 are assigned, including invoice download and usage display.
Each feature says what it takes in and what it exposes, for example the grant-limits call, the quote call, or the usage counts handed to entitlements.
Each feature can be tested alone, for instance with a fake of the other service, and the answer does not rely on the other side being finished.
Each feature is given its own section with scope, stories, components, dependencies and owner or TBD, followed by a separate closing list of the contracts that several features use.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The HLD contains a cycle spread over several bullet points: Billing calls Entitlements and Entitlements calls Billing. A split by service would produce cyclic dependence.

scenarios.title: Everything revolves around the order entity
scenarios.prompt:
We're rebuilding the order management part of our B2B wholesale portal. Please split the project into features my team of five can each take. Design notes below.

Core entity: Order (id, customer, lines, status, totals, shipping address, payment state).

Parts that touch Order:
- Order creation from cart / reorder from history
- Pricing and discount calculation (writes totals)
- Fulfilment: warehouse picks, packs, ships (writes status, shipping)
- Invoicing and payment reconciliation (writes payment state)
- Returns and refunds (writes status, totals)
- Customer order history & search (reads everything)
- Email notifications on status changes
- Sales rep dashboard showing open orders by customer

Stories:
1 Buyer places an order from cart
2 Buyer reorders a past order
3 Buyer sees volume discounts applied
4 Warehouse marks order shipped with tracking
5 Finance reconciles payments to invoices
6 Buyer requests a return and gets a refund
7 Buyer searches order history
8 Buyer is emailed when status changes
9 Sales rep sees open orders for their accounts
rubric: Notes that many features write the same Order record (pricing, fulfilment, invoicing, returns) and proposes a dedicated first piece of work that defines the Order schema and status lifecycle, rather than having each feature edit it.
Names the common contract (Order fields and status values, or events on status change) and lists which features use it.
All nine stories are placed in a feature.
Features are vertical business capabilities such as fulfilment or returns and refunds with their own storage, logic and screens, not layers.
Says the Order definition is done first and proposes an order of the other features or who can start in parallel afterwards.
Features such as returns or search can be verified against sample orders without the other features being complete.
Asks the user to confirm or adjust the proposed split.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Four features write one entity and three read it, so the situation calls for a dedicated first piece of work over the shared data model.

scenarios.title: One huge area and several trivial ones
scenarios.prompt:
Hey, can you decompose this internal HR portal project into tasks for our engineers? We have 3 devs and roughly 8 weeks.

Rough scope with my own guesses at effort:
- Payroll engine: tax rules for 6 countries, overtime, bonuses, retro-pay, payslip generation, bank file export. (I'd say 3 months for one person, maybe more)
- Update personal details form (half a day)
- Show company holiday calendar (1 day)
- Leave requests and approval by manager (2 weeks)
- Download employment letter as PDF (1 day)
- Org chart view (3 days)
- Single sign-on with our identity provider (1 week)

Stories:
H1 Employee updates their address and phone
H2 Employee sees holiday calendar
H3 Employee requests leave and manager approves
H4 Employee downloads employment letter
H5 Employee browses org chart
H6 Employee views and downloads payslips
H7 Payroll admin runs monthly payroll
H8 Employee logs in with company SSO
rubric: Does not leave the payroll engine as one assignment of about three months; breaks it into pieces such as country tax rules, overtime and bonuses, payslips, and bank export that fit a couple of weeks each.
Combines the tiny items (personal details, holiday calendar, employment letter, org chart) into one or two employee self-service features instead of giving each its own owner.
All eight stories H1 to H8 are placed, including payslip download and SSO.
Offers an order or effort view across the three developers within the eight weeks, such as SSO early because others need login.
Says what the payroll pieces consume and produce, for example tax rule output feeding payslip generation.
Payroll pieces and self-service features can each be checked on their own, for example with fixed sample pay data.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The effort guesses show a very large item and several tiny ones, so the sizing of each feature matters alongside coverage.

scenarios.title: Ride-sharing notes with overlooked cross-cutting stories
scenarios.prompt:
ok so here's our ride share MVP planning doc, pasted straight from Notion. can you split it up into features so we can hand them out? we are 4 people.

Architecture: mobile apps (rider, driver), API gateway, Trips service, Matching service, Payments (Stripe Connect), Notifications (push), Postgres + Redis.

User stories
R1 Rider requests a ride with pickup and drop-off
R2 Rider sees nearby drivers and a fare estimate before requesting
R3 Driver goes online/offline and receives ride offers
R4 Driver accepts, navigates, completes trip
R5 Rider pays automatically at trip end; driver gets payout weekly
R6 Rider and driver rate each other
R7 Rider gets push notification when driver arrives
R8 Rider can cancel; cancellation fee after 2 minutes
R9 Support can look up any trip and issue a refund
R10 Driver onboarding: upload licence and vehicle docs, admin approves
R11 All personally identifiable data (phone, location history) is deleted on account deletion request
R12 Rider can share live trip link with a friend

Note from PM: R11 and R12 are "later but must be in the plan". Also, trips and matching both need to read driver location in Redis.
rubric: All twelve stories appear in the split, including cross-cutting R11 (data deletion) and later items R12 and R10, and none is dropped for being later.
Picks up that trip and matching features both rely on driver location in Redis and either merges them or names a driver-location contract and the features that use it.
Features are vertical flows such as rider booking, driver side and onboarding, payments and payout, support tools, and not layers like apps, API, services, database.
States inputs, outputs or interfaces for the main features, such as ride offer, trip status, payment event.
Suggests what is defined first and a rough sequence, and treats R11 and R12 as later in the order but still covered.
Each feature can be verified alone, for instance using a fake location feed or a stub payment.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Twelve stories include cross-cutting deletion, an onboarding flow far from the core, and a shared Redis location note buried in a footer. Coverage and shared-data are easy to miss.

scenarios.title: Small team, user account core shared by three tracks
scenarios.prompt:
I run a small edtech startup. We're building a learning platform and I need the work divided up so three contractors can work without stepping on each other. Design is below.

Everything hangs off the User table (id, role: student/teacher/admin, email, profile, org_id).

Modules:
1. Courses: teachers create courses, lessons, quizzes (reads User for teacher ownership)
2. Enrollment & progress: students enroll, progress percentages, certificates (reads/writes User profile completion field, reads Course)
3. Classroom messaging: threads between students and teachers (reads User)
4. Billing: course purchases and teacher payouts (writes User billing status)
5. Admin: user management, roles, suspensions (writes User)

Stories:
E1 Teacher builds a course with video lessons and quizzes
E2 Student enrolls and tracks progress
E3 Student gets a certificate on completion
E4 Student messages the teacher
E5 Student buys a course
E6 Teacher receives monthly payout
E7 Admin suspends a user
E8 Admin changes a user's role
rubric: Sees that enrollment, billing and admin all write the User record and proposes one early dedicated piece of work that fixes the User fields, roles and statuses so contractors do not each alter the record.
Names the User contract (and possibly the Course reference) and lists which of the three contractors' features consume it.
Gives three contractors self-contained feature tracks, for example courses and quizzes, learning and certificates, commerce and payouts, not data/backend/frontend groupings.
All eight stories E1 to E8 are covered, including messaging and role changes.
Does not create a loop such as courses needing enrollment while enrollment needs courses; if mentioned, resolves it with a shared contract.
Presents the split as something for the user to confirm or change before assigning contractors.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: A User record that three modules write is the key situation; with three contractors the split must avoid collisions.

scenarios.title: IoT fleet monitoring split with sizing and order
scenarios.prompt:
We're doing a fleet monitoring platform for refrigerated trucks. Please break the project down into pieces my five engineers can pick up, and tell me what should happen first. Design below:

- Device firmware gateway ingests MQTT temperature/GPS messages, validates and writes to a time-series store (Timescale). Estimated 4 weeks, includes device provisioning and certificates.
- Alert rules engine: thresholds per truck/cargo type, evaluates the stream, raises alerts. 3 weeks.
- Notifications: sends SMS/email for alerts and escalates if unacknowledged. 1 week.
- Live map dashboard: truck positions, filters. 3 weeks.
- Temperature history reports with PDF export for compliance audits. 2 weeks.
- Customer-facing API with API keys for third parties to pull data. 2 weeks.
- Account and fleet management (customers, trucks, drivers, permissions). 3 weeks.

Stories:
F1 Dispatcher sees live truck positions
F2 Dispatcher gets alerted when cargo temp leaves range
F3 Alert escalates if nobody acknowledges
F4 Compliance officer exports temperature history for an audit
F5 Fleet manager adds trucks and assigns drivers
F6 Third-party system pulls telemetry via API
F7 Admin configures thresholds per cargo type
F8 New device is provisioned and starts reporting
rubric: Gives an order based on dependencies, for example telemetry message format and fleet/truck identity settled first, ingestion and account management early, alerts and dashboard after.
Identifies the telemetry record format and truck/fleet identity as used by ingestion, alerts, map, reports and API, and says to define them up front.
Because several features read the same truck and telemetry data, proposes a dedicated first piece of work that defines it.
All eight stories F1 to F8 are mapped, with thresholds (F7) and provisioning (F8) in a feature.
Says what each piece consumes and produces, such as the alert event passed to notifications.
Each piece can be tested alone, for example with recorded telemetry replayed into the alert engine.
Each feature is its own section with scope, stories, components, dependencies and owner or TBD, then a separate closing list of the contracts that several features use.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Sizes are already given and mostly within range; the question stresses order and the shared telemetry and truck data across many parts.
